title: Admission of a Partner
summary: A new partner is admitted with the consent of all existing partners and acquires a share of profits and a share in the firm's assets. This chapter covers calculation of the new and sacrificing ratios, treatment of goodwill as per AS-26 (including hidden goodwill), revaluation, reserves, and adjustment of partners' capitals.

notes.heading: Admission and the adjustments required
notes.html:
A new partner may be admitted to bring in additional capital or skills. He can be admitted only with the consent of all existing partners (unless the deed provides otherwise). On admission the new partner gets two main rights: (1) a share in the assets of the firm and (2) a share in future profits.

Adjustments required on admission:

  1. Calculation of the new profit-sharing ratio and the sacrificing ratio
  2. Treatment of goodwill
  3. Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities
  4. Distribution of accumulated profits, reserves and losses
  5. Adjustment of partners' capitals (if required)

notes.heading: Calculating the new profit-sharing ratio
notes.html:
CaseIllustration (A and B share 3:2)New ratio
(a) Only the new partner's share is given; nothing said about how it is acquiredC gets 1/5. Remaining 4/5 is shared 3:2: A 3/5 x 4/5 = 12/25; B 2/5 x 4/5 = 8/25; C 5/2512:8:5 (old partners keep old ratio between them)
(b) New partner acquires specific fractions from old partnersC gets 1/5: 2/15 from A and 1/15 from B. A 9/15 − 2/15 = 7/15; B 6/15 − 1/15 = 5/15; C 3/157:5:3
(c) Old partners surrender a fraction of their own sharesA surrenders 1/3 of his share (3/5 x 1/3 = 1/5) and B 1/4 of his share (2/5 x 1/4 = 1/10). C = 1/5 + 1/10 = 3/10; A 3/5 − 1/5 = 4/10; B 2/5 − 1/10 = 3/104:3:3
(d) New partner's share is given and old partners' new ratio is also givenCalculate directly from the information—

Sacrificing ratio = Old ratio − New ratio for each old partner. In case (a) it equals the old ratio (3:2); in case (b) it is 2/15 : 1/15 = 2:1; in case (c) it is 1/5 : 1/10 = 2:1.

notes.heading: Treatment of goodwill (premium method as per AS-26)

notes.heading: Hidden goodwill
notes.html:
When the value of goodwill is not given, it is inferred from the capital brought in by the new partner.

  1. Total capital of the new firm (implied) = New partner's capital x Reciprocal of his share.
  2. Actual total capital = Old partners' capitals after all adjustments (revaluation, reserves) + New partner's capital.
  3. Hidden goodwill of the firm = (1) − (2). New partner's share of goodwill = Hidden goodwill x his share.

Worked illustration 2

A and B have capitals (after adjustments) of ₹1,20,000 and ₹80,000. C brings ₹1,00,000 for 1/4 share. Implied capital = 1,00,000 x 4 = ₹4,00,000. Actual capital = 1,20,000 + 80,000 + 1,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Hidden goodwill = ₹1,00,000; C's share = ₹25,000, debited to C's Current A/c and credited to sacrificing partners.

notes.heading: Revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits
notes.html:
• Gains and losses on revaluation belong to the old partners in the old ratio; the new partner should neither benefit nor suffer from changes that took place before his admission. A Revaluation Account is prepared exactly as in a change of ratio.
  • General reserve, credit balance of P&L, workmen compensation reserve (excess over claim) and investment fluctuation reserve (excess over fall in value) are credited to old partners in the old ratio.
  • Debit balance of P&L and deferred revenue expenditure are debited to old partners in the old ratio.
  • If the partners want reserves to remain in the books, the new partner's capital is debited and the old partners are credited in the sacrificing ratio for his share (a single adjusting entry).

notes.heading: Comprehensive worked illustration
notes.html:
A and B share 3:2. Balance Sheet on 31 March 2025: Creditors ₹60,000; General Reserve ₹30,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,00,000 (total ₹3,40,000). Assets: Cash ₹40,000; Debtors ₹80,000; Stock ₹70,000; Machinery ₹1,50,000 (total ₹3,40,000). C is admitted for 1/4 share on 1 April 2025 and brings ₹1,00,000 as capital and ₹40,000 as premium. Stock is reduced by 10%, machinery appreciated by ₹20,000 and a provision for doubtful debts of ₹4,000 is created.

Revaluation Account: Gain on machinery 20,000 − loss on stock 7,000 − provision 4,000 = profit ₹9,000 (A ₹5,400; B ₹3,600).

Premium: sacrificing ratio = old ratio 3:2 (no other information), so A ₹24,000 and B ₹16,000.

notes.heading: Adjustment of capitals
notes.html:
(1) New partner's capital based on old partners' capitals: Total capital of new firm = Combined adjusted capitals of old partners x Reciprocal of their combined new share. New partner's capital = Total capital x his share. Example: adjusted capitals A ₹1,20,000 + B ₹80,000 = ₹2,00,000 for 4/5 share; C is admitted for 1/5. Total capital = 2,00,000 x 5/4 = ₹2,50,000; C's capital = ₹50,000.

(2) Old partners' capitals based on new partner's capital: Total capital = New partner's capital x Reciprocal of his share; each old partner's required capital = Total capital x his new share. Surplus is withdrawn (or credited to current account) and deficit is brought in.

Worked illustration 3

In the comprehensive illustration, C brings ₹1,00,000 for 1/4 share, so total capital = ₹4,00,000. Required: A 9/20 = ₹1,80,000; B 6/20 = ₹1,20,000. A has ₹1,97,400, so A withdraws ₹17,400; B has ₹1,31,600, so B withdraws ₹11,600. Entry: A's Capital A/c Dr 17,400; B's Capital A/c Dr 11,600 To Cash A/c 29,000.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Crediting premium to old partners in the old ratio when the sacrificing ratio is different.
  • Sharing revaluation profit with the new partner.
  • Raising goodwill in the books instead of using the premium method.
  • Forgetting to write off existing goodwill (old ratio) before recording the premium.
  • Calculating hidden goodwill using capitals before revaluation and reserve adjustments.
  • Recording an entry when premium is paid privately.

keyTerms.definition: Entry of a new partner into an existing firm with the consent of all partners; a form of reconstitution.
Ratio in which all partners, including the incoming partner, share future profits.
Ratio in which old partners give up their shares in favour of the new partner; used to distribute premium for goodwill.
Amount brought by the new partner as compensation to sacrificing partners for his share of goodwill.
Method prescribed in line with AS-26 under which goodwill is not raised but the new partner's share is credited to sacrificing partners.
Goodwill inferred as the excess of the capital implied by the new partner's contribution over the actual total capital of the firm.
Account recording changes in values of assets and liabilities on admission; its profit or loss is shared by old partners in old ratio.
Account debited with the new partner's share of goodwill when he does not bring premium in cash.
Capital of each partner kept in proportion to his new profit-sharing ratio.
Premium paid by the new partner directly to old partners outside the firm; not recorded in the firm's books.

formulas.name: New share of an old partner
formulas.html: Old share − Share surrendered to the new partner

formulas.name: New ratio when only new partner's share is given
formulas.html: Old partner's new share = Old share x (1 − New partner's share)

formulas.name: Sacrificing ratio
formulas.html: Old ratio − New ratio (for each old partner)

formulas.name: New partner's share of goodwill
formulas.html: Firm's goodwill x New partner's share

formulas.name: Firm's goodwill from premium
formulas.html: Premium brought by new partner x Reciprocal of his share

formulas.name: Hidden goodwill
formulas.html: (New partner's capital x Reciprocal of his share) − (Adjusted capitals of old partners + New partner's capital)

formulas.name: New partner's capital based on old capitals
formulas.html: Combined adjusted capital of old partners x Reciprocal of their combined new share x New partner's share

formulas.name: Total capital based on new partner's capital
formulas.html: New partner's capital x Reciprocal of his share; Old partner's required capital = Total capital x his new share

mcqs.q: A and B share profits 3:2. C is admitted for 1/4 share. The new profit-sharing ratio will be:
Premium for goodwill brought by a new partner is credited to:
options: All partners in the new ratio
Old partners in the old ratio in every case
Sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio
New partner's capital account
mcqs.explanation: The premium compensates those who sacrifice their share, in the proportion of their sacrifice.

mcqs.q: A and B have adjusted capitals of ₹50,000 and ₹30,000. C brings ₹40,000 for 1/4 share. Hidden goodwill of the firm is:

Assertion (A): When a new partner is unable to bring his share of goodwill in cash, his current account is debited.
Reason (R): AS-26 does not permit raising of self-generated goodwill in the books.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Because goodwill cannot be raised, the only way to compensate sacrificing partners is to debit the new partner's current account; R explains A.

mcqs.q: Case: X and Y share profits equally. Z is admitted for 1/3 share and brings ₹60,000 as capital and ₹30,000 as his share of goodwill. The value of the firm's goodwill is:
mcqs.explanation: Z's share ₹30,000 is for 1/3; firm's goodwill = 30,000 x 3 = ₹90,000.

mcqs.q: Goodwill already appearing in the books at the time of admission of a partner is written off among:
options: Old partners in old ratio
All partners in new ratio
Old partners in sacrificing ratio
All partners equally
mcqs.explanation: Existing goodwill belongs to the old partners and is written off in their old ratio.

mcqs.q: Adjusted capitals of A and B are ₹1,20,000 and ₹80,000. C is admitted for 1/5 share. C's capital, on the basis of the old partners' capitals, should be:
mcqs.explanation: ₹2,00,000 represents 4/5; total capital = ₹2,50,000; C's capital = 2,50,000 x 1/5 = ₹50,000.

mcqs.q: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5 share, taking 2/15 from A and 1/15 from B. The sacrificing ratio is:

Assertion (A): Premium for goodwill paid privately by the new partner to old partners is recorded in the firm's books.
Reason (R): Such premium does not pass through the business.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Since the money does not come into the firm, no entry is passed; A is false and R is true.

mcqs.q: At the time of admission, profit on revaluation of assets and liabilities is credited to:
options: All partners, including the new partner, in new ratio
Old partners in old ratio
Old partners in sacrificing ratio
New partner only
mcqs.explanation: The change in values relates to the period before admission, so it belongs to old partners in old ratio.

mcqs.q: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted; A surrenders 1/3 of his share and B surrenders 1/4 of his share in favour of C. The new ratio is:
mcqs.explanation: A gives 1/5 and B gives 1/10; C = 3/10, A = 4/10, B = 3/10. Ratio 4:3:3.

mcqs.q: Case: C's share of goodwill on admission is ₹30,000, but he brings only ₹18,000 in cash. The amount to be debited to C's current account is:
options: Nil
mcqs.explanation: The unpaid portion 30,000 − 18,000 = ₹12,000 is debited to C's current account.

questions.q: State any two rights acquired by a newly admitted partner.
questions.answerHtml:
• Right to share the assets of the firm.
  • Right to share the future profits of the firm.

questions.q: When is hidden goodwill calculated at the time of admission?
questions.answerHtml: When the value of goodwill is not given and has to be inferred from the capital brought in by the new partner for his share of profit.
